1.pericope_label: The monuments of idolatry to be destroyed, and the Lord not to be served in their manner

schools.summary: Gill takes the hills and green trees literally, reports the rabbinic reading that while heathen altars were to be overthrown not a stone might be removed from the house of God nor any of his names blotted out, and cites Maimonides that whoever takes a stone from the altar or temple in the way of destruction is to be beaten; Calvin makes the one sanctuary and one altar the chief external distinction between lawful worship and every fictitious Gentile rite, a barrier raised to separate the people from the world, and annexes the whole external profession of worship to the second commandment.

Henry sets the chapter under the second commandment as a hedge about the first, presses that the statutes bind in prosperity as well as in the wilderness and all the days we live on earth, observes that no idol temples are mentioned and takes this to support the view that the tabernacle was the first building raised for religious use, explains why height and shade were thought to help devotion while granting that a solemn grove is still admired, and adds that such places really served to conceal works of darkness that could not bear the light.

Clarke summarises the whole chapter and then expounds the objects of destruction one by one, the altars of unholy sacrifice, the pillars cut from stone, the groves like those about the temple of Ashtaroth where impure rites were practised, and the images carved in wood, and explains that the names of the gods were graven on stones and trees and thence passed to whole mountains, valleys and districts; Wesley glosses the places as temples, chapels and altars, and takes the pillars for the supports on which images stood.

Ellicott gives the substitution of bosheth for baal in Jerubbaal, Eshbaal and Meribbaal as a literal fulfilment of the command to destroy the names, while allowing that it may answer rather to the parallel in Exodus, and answers the objection that the command belongs to a later age by showing that its execution was bound up with the conquest in detail, so that each tribe was left to cleanse its own portion, with the alarm over the altar Ed as evidence that early Israel had no leaning to idolatry; Keil and Delitzsch describe the plan of the second half of the address, and draw out the contrast between the heathen who seeks nature-gods wherever he discerns a trace of divinity and the God who has fixed for himself a name in which he dwells among his people, presented in a visible sign that was during the journeying the pillar of cloud and fire.

debates: Whether the command to destroy the monuments betrays a later date, which Ellicott denies by tying its execution to the piecemeal conquest
What the destroying of the names means: Clarke refers it to place-names taken from the gods, Ellicott to the later substitution of bosheth for baal in personal names
outliers: Henry infers from the silence about idol temples that the tabernacle may have been the first building ever raised for religious use, and that temples took their rise from it
Gill records the rabbinic counterpart of the command, that a man is beaten for removing so much as a stone from the temple by way of destruction

5.pericope_label: The one chosen place, the gifts brought thither, and the joy of the sacrificial meal

schools.summary: Gill enumerates the offerings, glosses the rest and the inheritance, and observes from the mention of daughters that women came up to the feasts; Calvin asks why sacrifice was confined to one altar and answers that the place stood like a standard to gather believers into the unity of faith while the reserved choice commended obedience, raises the difficulty that the ark had no fixed resting-place before David and answers that the place was not chosen until it was set in Zion, presses the words out of all your tribes as marking a privilege given to one tribe and withheld from the rest, and takes the sanctuary for the place where God manifested himself present so that the meal was a communion.

Henry observes that no precept in the law is so largely pressed as this and gives three reasons, the people's proneness to idolatry, the usefulness of one place for keeping corrupt customs out and preserving unity, and the significancy of the appointment as a token that there is one God and one Mediator, adds that it bound the sacrifices only since men might pray everywhere as in the synagogues, and dwells on the note of gladness, that the service was to be a pleasure and not a task.

Clarke explains why uniformity was then essential, every rite having a determinate meaning and pointing to things to come, so that without one place the representative system would have been destroyed and the Messiah could not have been seen through the ritual, and adds that the same necessity does not now exist since the shadows have fled, though it remains desirable that Christians glorify their Lord with one mouth; Wesley explains the putting of the name as setting up worship in a house called by God's name, first at Shiloh and then at Jerusalem, guards that the eating was not in the most holy place, and infers from the daughters that women came up.

Ellicott argues that the very form of the order proves its antiquity, since no one acquainted with the removal of the place from Shiloh to Nob, Gibeon and Jerusalem could have written so unconscious of later history, notes that the Jews of our Lord's day had reached the same unconsciousness and appeals to Stephen's speech, finds in the words about doing as they do here a mark of the wilderness condition, insists that the law of Moses has a prophetic side given when Israel could not yet keep it, and supports this from the neglect of booths at Tabernacles from Joshua to Nehemiah; Keil and Delitzsch classify the gifts in four pairs, argue that the tithes meant are not the vegetable tithes only, and describe the sacrificial meals as the visible expression of a people's joy at their God's table.

debates: When the place was chosen: Calvin holds that it was not chosen until the ark rested in Zion, and reads the psalms accordingly, while Ellicott takes the unconsciousness of Shiloh, Nob and Gibeon as proof that the command was written long before any of them
Which tithes are meant, Keil and Delitzsch denying that the vegetable tithes alone are in view
outliers: Ellicott insists on a prophetic side to the law of Moses, given at a time when Israel was not in a position to keep it, and finds the Jews' own neglect of booths from Joshua to Nehemiah in point
Clarke argues that the reason for uniformity has lapsed with the shadows, while wishing for it still on other grounds

15.pericope_label: Eating flesh in the gates, the blood poured out, and the Levite not forsaken

schools.summary: Gill relieves the common table of the sanctuary, distinguishes the third-year tithe laid up within the gates from the Levites' own portion, and reads forsaking the Levite as neglecting to bring him to the feast rather than merely withholding his maintenance; Calvin grounds the blood prohibition in its pre-Mosaic history, arguing that it had fallen into desuetude and was ratified anew as a mark of separation, that its reason is that the blood is the life, and that its true object is that cruelty might be abhorred, since the severity of the punishment is out of proportion to the act itself.

Ellicott reads the permission as a deliberate modification of Leviticus 17:3-4, whose continuance in Canaan would have stopped the eating of flesh altogether, takes the frequent mention of roebuck and hart as evidence that hunting was familiar in the wilderness, follows the Jewish commentators in identifying the second tithe, and makes the pouring out of the blood a sacramental reminder of the death of Christ; Keil and Delitzsch describe the earth receiving the blood into its bosom and restate that sacrificial meals belonged to the sanctuary alone.

Clarke identifies the roebuck as an antelope on Dr Shaw's authority, argues that the command concerns only tame beasts used for food since game shot with arrows could not have its blood poured at the altar, rejects Calmet's reading that pouring the blood as water means pouring it without ceremony, and turns the charge about the Levite into a rule that those who serve God at the altar should be furnished with the necessaries of life; Wesley glosses within thy gates as the private habitations set over against the place of worship.

debates: Whether pouring the blood out as water describes the manner (Calmet, that it was done without ceremony) or the intent (Clarke, that it was poured by way of sacrifice)
What the blood is the life means: Augustine, as Calvin reports him, took it for the sign of life, while Calvin holds that Moses means animal life is actually contained in the blood
Which tithe is forbidden in the gates: Gill the third-year tithe, Ellicott with the Jewish commentators the second tithe
outliers: Calvin argues that the blood law was given to Noah, lapsed among the nations, and is questionable even among the family of Shem, so that its renewal is effectively a fresh promulgation
Ellicott notes that the Levites kept their provision in Israel only until Jeroboam and his sons cast them off, after which they migrated to Judah
No block-keying loss can be repaired here: Matthew Henry keys his notes to verses 1 and 5 only, so the whole of this section is without his comment

20.pericope_label: The enlarged border, the licence to kill at home, and the blood prohibition repeated

schools.summary: Gill reads the enlarged border of the pastures of Canaan, presses the conditional particle as meaning seeing the place will be too far, gathers the rabbinic readings of the holy things from Onkelos, Jonathan and Aben Ezra, and supplies the sanction that God threatened to set his face against the blood-eater; Calvin explains why so earnest an exhortation to firmness was needed, since the precept was trifling in appearance, troublesome to keep and everywhere neglected by the Gentiles, restates the purpose of the single altar lest many altars beget many gods, and warns that the promised reward does not of itself move men but is an indulgence to believers whose defects are not imputed.

Ellicott reads verses 20-25 as an expansion of 15-16 and a modification of the stricter Levitical rule, the distance to the sanctuary making universal feasting there impossible, suggests that the promise contemplates a physical as well as a moral effect, distinguishes the holy things as firstlings and second tithe from the first tithe which was not holy, and identifies the sacrifices of verse 27 as peace offerings; Keil and Delitzsch render the imperative as be strong not to eat the blood, gloss alike as together without requiring clean and unclean to eat in company, and note that vows are joined to the holy gifts as springing from spontaneous impulse.

Wesley traces the release to a scruple, that men obliged to bring their sacrifices to the tabernacle might think themselves bound to bring all their cattle, and notes that the far case alone is mentioned though the liberty holds near and far; he explains that the unclean were not excluded because there was no holiness in such meat, and excepts from the flesh eaten what was burned to God's honour or given to the priest. Clarke supplies the reason from Leviticus, that the blood is the life and the life was offered as an atonement.

debates: Whether the promise that it may go well with thee looks to moral consequences only or, as Ellicott suggests, to physical ones as well
What the holy things comprise: Onkelos and Jonathan the tithe, Aben Ezra the burnt and peace offerings, Gill all of them together, Ellicott the firstlings and the second tithe
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch guard the word rendered alike, warning that it means the one just as the other and does not require the clean to eat in company with the unclean
Calvin traces the temptation to a specific piece of reasoning, that a man who judged abstinence from blood to contribute nothing to holiness would find in that judgment a snare to indulgence
Matthew Henry keys his notes to verses 1 and 5 only, so this whole section stands without his comment and the loss cannot be repaired

29.pericope_label: Do not enquire after their gods; add not to the word, nor diminish from it

schools.summary: Gill names the seven nations, reads the snare as their examples and customs, and takes the closing rule to bind both matter and manner, so that nothing heathen is added and nothing enjoined neglected; Calvin makes the enquiry itself the origin of idolatry, since men dissatisfied with the simplicity of God's worship are drawn by the snares of novelty, argues from the philology that possess them before thy face means the land is left vacant rather than the nations enslaved, defends the received rendering of the snare against better-construed alternatives, and turns the final clause into a rule that obedience is the mother of piety and every self-devised worship a false god, applying the threatening of Isaiah 29 to the ceremonies of the Papal church.

Keil and Delitzsch place the warning as a transition from the true mode of worship to the laws about tempters to idolatry in chapter 13, summarise the ground of the prohibition in the abominations the Canaanites prepared for their gods and the children they burnt to Moloch, and prefer to read verse 32 as an intermediate link rather than, with many commentators, as the conclusion of the preceding chapter; Ellicott confirms the caution from Jeremiah, where Israel still had to be warned against the dread of heathen deities attached to their seats of worship, and argues that no later writer could have put the words about adding and diminishing into the mouth of Moses if he had himself altered the precepts appreciably.

Wesley locates the danger precisely, in the example the nations left behind them once their persons were destroyed. Clarke observes that almost all the nations of the world agreed in offering human victims on extraordinary occasions, infers that none of them had any right notion of the divine nature, and uses this to argue how necessary revelation was to teach men what religion can please God, pressing the point against those who profess Christianity yet oppose sending the gospel abroad.

debates: Whether verse 32 closes the preceding chapter or opens what follows: Keil and Delitzsch report the first as the view of many commentators and prefer the second
How the word rendered snared should be construed: Calvin reports renderings that suit the construction better but keeps the received one for the aptness of the metaphor
outliers: Calvin insists that Moses does not say the nations were to be possessed as slaves taken in war, but that the land would lie vacant once they were destroyed
Clarke turns the ancient practice of human sacrifice into a contemporary argument for foreign missions, naming the offerings still made to Cali and at Jaggernaut
Matthew Henry keys his notes to verses 1 and 5 only, so this closing section stands without his comment and the loss cannot be repaired
